name: Defensive Attribution Hypothesis
description: When judging an accident or misfortune, people can assign less blame to actors they identify with and more blame to targets who feel unlike them. The attribution protects the observer's own sense that they would be safe or justified in a similar situation.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to safety incidents, trust-and-safety review, appeals, abuse reporting, fraud decisions, and internal postmortems. Teams can unconsciously soften judgments of actors who feel like 'people like us' or distance themselves from victims to preserve a sense of control.
prevalence_note: A real classic in social psychology and accident-blame research, but only occasionally named explicitly in product, UX, or service-design practice outside safety, moderation, or justice-adjacent work.

findings.description: Burger's meta-analysis of 22 peer-reviewed studies found strong cumulative support for the defensive-attribution hypothesis: when observers identified more with an accident actor or saw themselves as similarly situated, they attributed less blame and responsibility to that actor. The pattern supports a self-protective motivational asymmetry in responsibility judgments rather than a purely neutral causal reading of the event.
findings.source_title: Motivational biases in the attribution of responsibility for an accident: A meta-analysis of the defensive-attribution hypothesis.
